This fetch quest simulator will have you going back and forth through the same scenes over and over, occasionally having boring, uninspired fights along the way. You'll have this game mastered in about 30 minutes, since the maximum movement speed is dreadfully slow and the archery is more spray-and-pray than focused and precise. Speaking of movement, it's incredibly drifty in this game. If you're moving even a little quickly when you land on the ground and don't grapple something right away, you'll slide right off the edge. For a game that's built around small platforms and combat, I cannot possibly fathom why they chose to give the character nearly 0 friction. There's also no penalty for dying which, I believe, is motivated by the combat being so bad. You''ll rarely die from enemy attacks (at least as far as I've gotten into the game), but you'll likely die constantly from falling off small platforms as you try to hit small weakpoints on enemies who are shooting homing projectiles and jumping around the arena. Due to the map design surrounding the fights, you'll often find that, once you slip off an edge, there will be nothing to grapple onto as you fall for 3-4 seconds. 

I honestly cannot recommend anyone buy this game for less than half-off and, even then, only pick it up if you absolutely love archery, a simplistic art style, and swinging through the air.

Windlands 2 is an ambitious virtual reality action-adventure developed and published by Psytec Games Ltd that places freedom of movement at the very center of its design. Rather than treating locomotion as a necessary compromise in VR, the game embraces it as its defining feature, building an experience where swinging, gliding, and soaring through the air feels as important as combat or story progression. From the first moments, it becomes clear that Windlands 2 is less about standing still and more about inhabiting a world through momentum, height, and motion.

The core of the experience lies in its grappling hook traversal, which allows players to latch onto distant surfaces and propel themselves across vast environments with fluid, physics-driven motion. Learning how to chain swings together, manage momentum, and choose the right anchor points becomes a skill in itself, one that gradually transforms initial uncertainty into exhilarating confidence. Once mastered, movement feels liberating, turning traversal into a kind of aerial dance that encourages experimentation and exploration. The sense of scale achieved through this system is particularly striking in VR, as cliffs, ruins, and open skies feel genuinely towering and expansive.

Combat is designed to complement this constant movement rather than interrupt it. The introduction of ranged weaponry, primarily a bow, pushes players to fight while airborne, using speed and positioning as key defensive tools. Encounters often reward those who stay mobile, circling enemies or grappling to vantage points rather than standing their ground. Boss battles, in particular, emphasize this design philosophy, combining traversal challenges with precision shooting and situational awareness. While aiming and weapon handling can feel demanding depending on hardware and player comfort, the integration of combat with traversal creates moments that feel uniquely suited to VR.

Narratively, Windlands 2 offers more structure and presence than its predecessor, providing context for the world and the threats that inhabit it. Voice-acted characters and guided objectives help frame the journey, giving players a clearer sense of purpose as they move between regions. The story itself is serviceable rather than groundbreaking, but it succeeds in grounding the action and giving emotional weight to major encounters. Importantly, narrative elements rarely slow the pace; instead, they act as connective tissue between exploration and combat.

Exploration is richly supported through open-ended level design filled with optional challenges, hidden paths, collectibles, and traversal trials. Timed races and movement challenges encourage players to refine their skills and revisit earlier areas with greater mastery, while secrets tucked into vertical spaces reward curiosity and daring. This structure gives the world a sense of depth and replayability, making it feel less like a linear campaign and more like a playground built for movement enthusiasts.

One of the game’s standout features is its cooperative multiplayer, which allows up to four players to explore and fight together online. Sharing the experience transforms the tone of the game, turning solitary traversal into a social spectacle as players swing side by side, coordinate attacks, or simply race each other across the skyline. Co-op does introduce moments of chaos and occasional technical roughness, but the shared sense of speed and freedom often outweighs these issues, adding longevity and variety to the experience.

Visually, Windlands 2 adopts a stylized art direction that prioritizes clarity and scale over photorealism. Environments are colorful and readable even at high speeds, an important consideration given how quickly players move through the world. Ruins, natural landscapes, and towering structures are designed to be visually striking without overwhelming the player, maintaining orientation during rapid traversal. The audio design complements this well, using ambient sound and music to reinforce both the serenity of exploration and the intensity of combat.

Comfort is an unavoidable consideration in a VR game built around constant motion, and Windlands 2 makes an effort to address this through various locomotion and comfort options. Even so, its high-speed swinging and verticality can be challenging for players sensitive to motion sickness. Those comfortable with VR movement will likely find the experience thrilling, while newcomers may need time to acclimate or adjust settings to suit their tolerance.

Ultimately, Windlands 2 stands as one of the more distinctive VR experiences available, defined by its commitment to movement as a form of expression. It may not excel equally in every area, but its blend of exhilarating traversal, integrated combat, expansive environments, and cooperative play creates moments that feel genuinely impossible outside of virtual reality. For players who value freedom, verticality, and the physical sensation of motion in VR, it delivers a memorable adventure that invites you not just to explore a world, but to fly through it.

Rating: 7/10

This is a pretty fun, chill game, but it's also not gonna blow your socks off. I played through it with a friend in co-op and I think this is the best way to play if possible. The premise is simple; you swing around to get from point A to point B, then shoot some enemies with the bow and do it all over again. The game is overall quite easy and there's only a few tricky traversal sections.

My main criticism of the game is that despite its rather short runtime, the game can sometimes feel like it's getting boring/dragging. Some of the boss fights can take a really long time with all of the shields you need to destroy and you will spend the game killing the same 3 or so enemies. There's also quite a bit of backtracking and sometimes the quest marker is not super clear where you need to go. I also found the first game had a more "zen" vibe to it similar to Journey or Abzu that this sequel lacks.

The act of just swinging around like spiderman, however, is truly fun in and of itself and thinking about how you are going to fling yourself to the next point can be really enjoyable. Firing the bow mid air and landing the perfect shot from across the map can also be very satisfying.

There are only about 15 min of actual gameplay here, but hours of NPC's sending you across the map just so that once you arrive there they can tell you to come back now.

The worst part though is as you progress through the game, there is less and less to grapple to, i guess to make it harder? So instead of feeling like you can freely explore the world, you instead become confined to these narrow paths of grapple points.

После первой локации игра превращается в платформер где ты стратегически пытаешься добраться до своей цели, вместо фановых полетов на своем граплхуке акий спайдермэн. 
И это еще не критично, но вот что игру делает действительно плохой - это БОССЫ. Хуже боссов не придумать. Во первых ваше ЕДИНСТВЕННОЕ вооружение это просто УЖАСНЫЙ лук, который имеет плохую баллистику, низкую скорость полета стрелы и его надо каждый раз дрочить что бы он выстрелил. Что бы нанести урон боссу нужно попасть в слабую зону, но боссы вертятся как ужи на сковородке, попутно атакуя вас обычно выписывая ваншот (если вы играете на средней сложности то иногда 2 попадания которые обычно идут одно за другим). У всех боссов 3 стадии, они все одинаковые за исключением некоторых слабых зон которые меняются, это мега скучно. Иногда боссы не дают вам встать на месте, что как бы нужно делать что бы использовать двуручный лук... какой выход? Представляю вам просто АФИГЕННЫЙ ГЕЙМПЛЕЙ: смерть - выстрел - смерть - выстрел. Молитесь что бы стрела попала в цель и босс не провернул финт который оставил бы вас баз урона. За мое первое прохождение я набил аж 250 смертей.... и это было так СКУЧНО просто выдрачивать 3 стадии босса, которые однотипные, попутно отвлекаясь на не менее скучных мобов. Это сделано только для того что бы увеличить время прохождения, не один человек на земле не сможет найти подобный гемплей фановым. Это вам не дарк соус где ты учишься на ошибках, нет, это дурка где ты бьешься головой об стену.
И да последние уровни игры, даже не учитывая боссов очень утомительны, а могла же быть годнота, ведь первый час игры реально драйвовый. 
Так что в итоге - не рекомендую эту игру, к сожалению.

It's unbelievable how badly this game gets one of its two core mechanics wrong. Movement is an absolute chore due to bad level design (targets way too small and far apart to hit without absolute precision) and the logistics of the mechanic itself: the delay to connecting to grapple points, the short distance you are able to latch on to things, and the overly complicated momentum logic. Technically speaking it all "makes sense" but it makes for a horribly un fun gameplay experience.

The other primary mechanic, archery, works well enough on the whole but it is absolutely dragged down by the above mentioned issues. Combat is rendered mostly simplistic due to an inability to move fluidly, and the few moments where the game wants you to move and shoot feel so cumbersome that in my playthrough I opted to take several deaths rather than bother playing the game the way the intended way.

Lastly this game has zero focus on making itself comfortable in VR. Between the "use joystick to move around" movement, several sections of the game that have you looking straight up with a heavy VR headset strapped to your head, and the nauseating rubber banding of the grappling hook (to say nothing of the memory leaks which caused heavy frame droppage multiple times during my playthrough) I'm surprised I managed to finish this game in spite of my relatively strong VR stomach.

I'd almost excuse a large portion of the objective flaws in this game given how old it is (a 2017 VR game is quite early in the scheme of things) but this is Windlands *2*. They had a chance to learn from their mistakes on the first entry in the series and clearly didn't bother to improve in any way shape or form.

Even at four and a half years after the game was released, this remains one of the best VR experiences I've ever had.

Some of the bosses can be tedious, and learning to juggle yourself between grapple points while attempting to shoot and enemy can be kind of difficult, but, in the end, you will accomplish some very rewarding tasks once you get better.

Starring Ganondorf who has allied himself with Hitler, Master Roshi with Hair, Tootsie-Roll Fro, and slug-people. You, and hopefully a friend or two, will embark on a journey well-made and thought out, ready for you to explore and experience.

Witness the finest grappling hook gameplay and be thankful there is an instant-suicide button as you traverse the way god intended: by flight. Jump from roof to roof and steal free cable for your friends as you discover what is bringing the evil to the Windlands, and why Ganondorf is suddenly into ethnic cleansing.
Using the power of your bow and physics, you will be tasked with fighting monstrosities ranging from an Abrams tank with spider’s legs to Shadow of the Colossus. There is no more satisfying feeling than the combat in this game, and there is no more satisfying exploration than the exhilaration you feel when playing this game.
Windlands 2 puts the wonder and mystery back in to games, and offers it all for you and a friend to enjoy for $30 full price, so let’s discuss what I don’t like.

The game has settings that are honestly kind of dumb, and equate to turning on the heater function of your computer. That’s right, the settings menu looking like stovetop burner dials wasn’t a coincidence, get the panini ready or your leftover pizza back in the delivery box: it’s baking time!
When you figure this out, you’ll save yourself some time and performance, and enjoy the game as-is. The only change I recommend actually altering is the render distance. You’ll want to see the sights this game has to offer.
There’s these little spike-ball-♥♥♥♥-things in the air that grow and shank you, throwing you off your grapple line if you get too close. These are used later in the game to force challenge upon the player. Hilariously enough, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who designed these has the same humor as God because they are the one grapple-able surface that doesn’t glow your chosen color when they are in range. This means that if you miss that far-shot you took and you have a window of opportunity that is purely nanoseconds between when you can grab something and when you’re too far is a matter of luck, guesswork, timing, and likely experience from the last three times you were thrown to your death. I wish the ‘crosshairs’ for the grappling hooks changed colors for these tricky little bastards.
Length: it’s too short.
This game can easily be beaten in a single sitting with a good friend, and I nearly did so. The gameplay itself is supposed to be extended by your difficulty in making jumps or completing courses, the boss fights get infinite respawns unless you turn on permadeath. This means that the game itself is naturally short and following this completion there’s no option for New Game+, if you want to play the game again your friend will have to start a new save or you will, no other choices. There’s races and other challenges you can do, but they’re ultimately hiding how short the game’s campaign is. I wish there was more of the campaign because I wanted more levels and variety to swing through, however I understand this isn’t easy and takes time. Why do I know that?


This game is a masterpiece, that’s why.

From the movement to the combat, from the story you can ignore or enjoy, from the exploration to the endgame this is what all games should aspire to make you feel in VR.

The levels are designed with intention, the bosses are within arenas that are fun, the story is so enjoyable you are left with longing for more. The only thing keeping you from enjoying this is your fear of heights and an entry fee of $30, $10 during a sale.
Stop doubting yourself, let yourself enjoy and fly free again. Remember who you are.

The movement mechanics are just a bit too demanding leading to a lot of kamikaze style fighting against the bosses, which do not regenerate their health when you die. The idea of swing parkouring around whilst taking bow shots at the enemies below is fun and randomly you may even land these streaks...

...but not very often due to some bad design decisions:
- You have to use both of your hands for shooting (because its a bow) meaning aiming time is done during a short free fall period.
- Enemies are below you whilst the grapple rope targets are above you so there is no good way to keep your focus on both at the same time.
- The movement becomes especially hard for those players who are restricted to do more controller turning instead of actually rotating their body due to cable length or play space limitations.
- This would have been easily fixable by at least giving an option for some grapple hook auto-aim to keep that momentum going.

The voiced dialogue for NPCs sometimes doesn't play if you are standing next to them. The voiced dialogue returns when you get away from the NPCs due to the system switching to their radio-chatter voice mode. You are still going to lose a lot of story bits because of this.

I really tried to like this game and pushed myself to play it but the frustration never really went away.

If you think this game might be for you, go play Jet Island instead. That game mixes large bosses, speedy grapple movement and combat wonderfully.

Windlands 1 and 2 are my favorite VR games, and I played a lot of games. So a review is long overdue.

Windlands 2 lets you be a superhero. If you merge Spiderman with Hawkeye, you get what you can do in Windlands 2.

Gameplay is the core that makes this game so good: The swinging physics are so intuitive and make so much fun, jumping around and shooting with a bow is just awesome. Archery and swinging are great VR activities!

The graphics, the style and the music are beautiful. There is some story which is not really important or outstanding, to be fair. But I prefer it this way, because it let's you play the game without pausing for some cutscenes and such.

More Features: A lot of checkpoints so you don't lose anything if you die, even bosses keep lost shields, a lot of hidden collectibles, avatar customization, additional modes (race/collect).

Recommendation: Play this game only if you have no VR sickness and if you are somewhat good in games in general. If you are a casual gamer whose only experince is candy crush and wii bowling and you want to see some VR, don't get this. This game is made for players who are at least decent in platformers and those who are will have a great time. The developers included some really good accessibility features, though.

Comparition to Windlands 1: The first one was neary zen-like, without dangers aside from falling. On its hardest difficulty it was a brutal platformer with parkour elements. Now Windlands 2 is another take on this formula, YES, it is different and you won't get more of exactly the same. There is fighing (=archery) - which is really cool as i mentioned - and the world feels more linear and unvaried compared to the first entry. Ah, and there is Multiplayer, which I did not test.

Negative aspects:
- You will see some routes multiple times (others call it backtracking) which can get a little bit tedious. But hey, swinging is fun even if you know the route.
- I think the jumping mechanic is somewhat weird and not always working properly. A walljump did a lot more in Game 1 and sometimes when I run fast, it just wouldnt jump high. But luckily checkpoints are really close to each other, so if you fall down, you won't lose more than a few seconds. Ah, and I was swinging 90% of the time and not running or jumping.

Wishes for a possible next entry: I would love some icy or snowy biotome! (Or a space world without gravity? Or some unrealistic swinging underwater?)
